name: The Linux Foundation
summary: The company-funded non-profit behind the CNCF, the PyTorch Foundation, OpenSearch, Valkey: nearly 1,500 project communities in all, most of them in sub-foundations with their own boards and rules.
intro: The Linux Foundation (LF) is a US non-profit formed in January 2007, when two industry consortia from 2000, the Open Source Development Labs and the Free Standards Group, merged. It is an Oregon mutual benefit corporation, tax-exempt under section 501(c)(6), the category for industry associations, not a 501(c)(3) charity like the Apache Software Foundation. Its members are companies, 2,126 of them in 2025, when its annual report forecast $311 million of revenue and said it served nearly 1,500 open-source project communities. It doesn’t own Linux itself: the name is a registered trademark of Linus Torvalds, whose work the foundation sponsors as one of its Fellows.

A “Linux Foundation project” rarely has “Linux” in its name. Most sit inside a sub-foundation with its own board, budget and members: Kubernetes in the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), PyTorch and Ray in the PyTorch Foundation, OpenStack in the OpenInfra Foundation. Others, such as Valkey, MLflow and the Xen Project, are hosted directly. What the label promises comes from the LF’s hosting rules: an open-source licence, a trademark and repositories held by the foundation rather than one company, and a technical process open to non-members. It doesn’t tell you the licence, the project’s maturity or how decisions are made; each sub-foundation and project writes its own charter.

For someone choosing a technology, the LF offers the same basic protection as the ASF, a neutral owner for the name, but by a different route. At the ASF individuals take part and companies get no seats; at the LF companies are the members, pay dues by tier, and sit on governing boards that set budgets, while maintainers and technical steering committees decide what goes into the code. That makes it the usual destination when competitors want to share a project one of them controlled, and when a community forks a project whose owner changed its licence: Valkey, the Redis fork, and OpenTofu, the Terraform fork, both started here, and AWS moved OpenSearch here in September 2024.

sections.title: Who pays and who votes
body: The bylaws set up three classes of voting members, Platinum, Gold and Silver, plus non-voting Associates. Each Platinum member appoints one director, up to 20; the Gold members as a class elect three directors and the Silver members one; and the board may add up to five at-large directors, one of them representing the Technical Advisory Board. Every member director must be an employee, officer or director of the company that put them there, and no more than two directors may come from the same corporate group. Members vote only where the bylaws require it; otherwise the board can amend the bylaws on its own.

Dues follow the tiers. A directed-fund agreement the LF published with the OpenSearch Software Foundation in 2024 lists them as $500,000 a year for Platinum, $100,000 for Gold and $5,000 to $20,000 for Silver depending on headcount; Associate membership, for non-profits, open-source projects and government bodies, is free. Sub-foundations charge their own dues on top.

In its 2025 annual report the LF forecast $311.3 million of revenue: $133.3 million from memberships and donations, $83.6 million from project services, $58.6 million from events and $29.6 million from training and certification. It expected to spend $284.8 million, $181.9 million of it on project support and $8.4 million on the Linux kernel project. A separate charity, LF Charities, is a 501(c)(3) supporting organisation for the LF and hosts Jupyter, Tazama and Moja Global.

sections.title: A foundation of foundations
body: A project at the LF usually has two legal halves. The money sits in a directed fund, which exists to “raise, budget and spend funds” for one technical project and has its own governing board and membership tiers; companies must already be LF members to join. The OpenSearch Software Foundation, whose charter took effect on September 16, 2024, is one: Premier members pay $150,000 a year and each appoint a board member, General members pay $5,000 to $40,000 by headcount and get one representative per five members (at most three), the chair of the technical steering committee sits on the board, and no corporate group may hold more than two seats. The LF keeps custody of and final authority over the money and charges a fee of 9% of the first $1 million raised each year and 6% above that.

The code sits in LF Projects, LLC, a Delaware series limited liability company in which each technical project is a separate “series”. That is why MLflow’s site says “MLflow Project, a Series of LF Projects, LLC” and Malloy’s says the same of Malloy. Each series has a technical charter, normally with a technical steering committee, and all of them follow LF Projects’ shared policies on antitrust, code of conduct and trademarks. A named sub-foundation such as the OpenSearch Software Foundation is this pair under one brand; the largest, like the CNCF, add their own technical committees and maturity stages.

To be hosted, a project has to use an open-source licence for its code (“e.g. OSI approved”), be supported by an LF member (the hosting page asks for at least one LF member and five organisations), let the foundation hold its trademark, domain and GitHub account, separate business governance from technical governance in a written charter, and let anyone participate in the technical community, which the LF calls “explicitly not pay-to-play”. In 2023 the LF said it held such assets for more than 980 projects, including over 700 trademark registrations and applications.

sections.title: How it differs from the ASF

items.name: Companies are members
items.text: The ASF’s members are individuals elected for their work, and no sponsor gets a say. The LF’s voting members are companies, and Platinum members each appoint a director. Paying doesn’t buy technical control, though: the hosting rules require technical decisions to be separate and open to non-members.

items.name: No single Way
items.text: Every ASF project follows the same rules: a PMC, lazy consensus on mailing lists, three binding votes per release, the Incubator before the top level. The LF has no common process. Each sub-foundation or project writes its own charter, and maturity ladders, where they exist, belong to sub-foundations such as the CNCF, which is why this page lists no stages.

items.name: Paid staff
items.text: The ASF pays nobody to work on its projects. The LF employs staff who run finance, events, marketing and infrastructure for projects, and sponsors developers through its Fellows programme, Linus Torvalds and Greg Kroah-Hartman among them in 2012.

sections.title: The main sub-foundations
sections.intro: Each has its own board, members and project rules. Valkey, DocumentDB, the Open Container Initiative, DPDK, Zephyr, MLflow, the Xen Project and many smaller projects sit outside these, hosted by the LF directly.

sections.title: Licences, and why forks land here
body: The LF has no licence of its own and doesn’t require one. Sub-foundations can: the CNCF charter says all new code comes in and goes out under the Apache License 2.0, with a Developer Certificate of Origin sign-off, unless its governing board grants an exception. It did so in March 2025, by majority vote, so OpenTofu could keep the MPL 2.0 when it joined the CNCF sandbox that April.

Because the trademark and repositories belong to the foundation rather than to a vendor, the LF is where communities have taken forks after a single owner changed a licence. OpenTofu was announced on September 20, 2023, after HashiCorp moved Terraform from MPL 2.0 to the Business Source License 1.1. Valkey followed on March 28, 2024, continuing from Redis 7.2.4 under the BSD 3-clause licence, backed by AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle, Ericsson and Snap. OpenSearch, which AWS had run since 2021, moved to its own LF foundation in September 2024. The LF’s 2025 annual report calls this the “Right to Fork” and credits Valkey with 50 contributing companies, 150 contributors and 13 releases, up to version 9.0; it also reports OpenSearch passing 900 million downloads, and a fork of Camunda, Fluxnova, started by five financial institutions under FINOS.

The same reasoning brings projects that were never relicensed. Companies also hand over projects they started so that competitors will contribute: Databricks gave MLflow to the LF in June 2020, Intel gave Cloud Hypervisor in December 2021, and CelerData gave StarRocks in early 2023 after moving it from the Elastic License to Apache 2.0.

story: In 2000 a consortium including HP, Intel, IBM and NEC set up the Open Source Development Lab to make Linux ready for enterprise computing; Linus Torvalds became its first fellow. The Free Standards Group, also from 2000, worked on Linux standards. On January 22, 2007 the two announced they would merge into the Linux Foundation, led by Jim Zemlin, who had run the Free Standards Group, with Fujitsu, Hitachi, HP, IBM, Intel, NEC, Novell and Oracle as founding platinum members.

Over the next decade the LF took on far more than Linux. As “Collaborative Projects” it took in the Xen hypervisor from Citrix in April 2013, the Cloud Foundry Foundation in December 2014 and the CNCF, formed around Kubernetes, in July 2015. Ceph and GraphQL foundations followed in 2018, OpenJS and Presto in 2019, OpenSSF in 2020 and PyTorch in 2022.

In the 2020s the LF became the usual home for forks after licence changes, OpenTofu in 2023 and Valkey in 2024, and for projects their creators wanted to make neutral, OpenSearch among them. In 2025 the OpenInfra Foundation, home of OpenStack, joined as a member foundation, the PyTorch Foundation took in vLLM, DeepSpeed and Ray, and the LF launched the Agentic AI Foundation around Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol. Its annual report forecast revenue above $310 million for the year.

choices.choice: An association funded by companies, not a charity
choices.why: Both founding groups were industry consortia, and the LF exists for companies that build on the same software to pay for it together; under 501(c)(6) its members are companies whose dues set their tier and board seats.

In the LF’s words, “no one company trusts another company to own assets for the community”: logos, trademarks, domains, repositories and CLAs are all seen as control points, so the foundation holds them for everyone.

choices.choice: Business and technical governance kept apart
choices.why: Paying members fund a project and sit on its governing board, so the hosting rules require a separate, open technical process that anyone can join without paying, to stop the project becoming pay-to-play.

choices.choice: A charter per project instead of one rulebook
choices.why: Projects arrive in all shapes: some raise money and have members, others don’t; some have thousands of developers, some a dozen; some write specifications rather than code. The LF says there is no “required” or “right” shape, so each writes its own charter.
